rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali argues that the hamzated form of nabiʾ preserves the word's original hamza, supported by Hijazi speakers who pronounce it.
rows.anchor: الحجة لمن همز النبيء أن يقول هو أصل الكلمة ألا ترى أن ناسا من أهل الحجاز حققوا الهمزة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report has the Prophet answer a man who called him nabīʾ Allah by saying he is nabī Allah.
rows.anchor: فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم: " لست نبيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author suspects some transmitters judged the report's chain weak.
rows.anchor: فأظن أن من أهل النقل من ضعف إسناد هذا الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As evidence against rejecting hamza, the author says a poet praised the Prophet with the plural and no known objection; a fault in the singular would also affect the plural.
rows.anchor: ولو كان في واحده نكير لكان الجمع كالواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who read without hamza cite the Quranic plural anbiyaʾ, whose pattern commonly comes from weak-final nouns, as evidence that the singular's hamza was replaced.
rows.anchor: وحجة من أبدل ولم يحقق مجيء الجمع في التنزيل على أنبياء

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh's report that all Arabs say tanabbaʾa with hamza supports deriving nabiʾ from the hamzated root and rules out nabāwa.
rows.anchor: سيبويه حكى أن جميع العرب يقولون تنبأ مسيلمة بالهمزة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows nabi to derive either from anbaʾa with hamza dropped through frequent use or from nabā, to rise.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج يجوز أن يكون نبي من أنبأت فترك همزته لكثرة الاستعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabrisī defines food as nourishment, ṭaʿm as eating, and food also as a physical substance perceived by taste.
rows.anchor: الطعام ما يتغذى به والطعم بضم الطاء الأكل والطعام عرض يدرك بحاسة الذوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wāḥid is the first number; God is one because He is distinguished by His most beautiful attributes.
rows.anchor: والله تعالى واحد لتفرده بصفاته الحسنى

rows.speaker: ابن السراج
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarraj derives duʿāʾ, supplication, from nidāʾ, calling.
rows.anchor: والدعاء أصله النداء عن ابن السراج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication is a request addressed by a speaker to someone above him; its distinction from a command lies in the speakers' rank.
rows.anchor: وحقيقة الدعاء قول القائل لمن فوقه افعل والفرق بينه وبين الأمر يظهر بالرتبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inbāt means bringing forth plants and derives from the sense of appearing.
rows.anchor: والإنبات إخراج النبات وأصله من الظهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baql is spring growth and, more specifically, any plant without a stem; both baqalat and abqalat are eloquent forms for the earth's producing it.
rows.anchor: فالبقل كل نبات ليس له ساق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qiththa has two pronunciations, with kasra on qaf preferred and identified as Quranic usage.
rows.anchor: وفي القثاء لغتان ضم القاف وكسرها والكسر أجود وهي لغة القرآن

rows.speaker: عيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: Isa al-Thaqafi is reported to have the anomalous reading with damma on qaf in qiththa.
rows.anchor: روي عن عيسى الثقفي في الشواذ بالضم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited verse depicts fūm as a crop cultivated in Medina.
rows.anchor: قد كنت أغنى الناس شخصا واحدا ورد المدينة عن زراعة فوم

rows.speaker: الفراء والأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Azhari say fūm means wheat or bread; Arabs use it to mean bake bread.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء والأزهري: هو الحنطة والخبز.

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some identify fūm as grains from which bread is baked.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم هو الحبوب التي تخبز

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says fūm means garlic, with fāʾ replacing thāʾ as in the words hadath and jadaf.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: هو الثوم أبدل من الثاء فاء كما قالوا حدث وجدف.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra considers the garlic reading more fitting because onion follows fūm in the verse.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: وهذا أشبه بما ذكره بعده من البصل

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj rejects garlic as an implausible meaning because people would not ask for garlic without bread, the staple.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وهذا بعيد لأنه لا يعرف الثوم بمعنى الفوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabrisī calls that objection weak because anomalous readings attributed to Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas read thūm, garlic, with thāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف لأنه قد روي في الشواذ عن ابن مسعود وابن عباس وثومها بالثاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAdas means the familiar lentil grain.
rows.anchor: والعدس حب معروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adnā can mean nearer or lower, as in something close or inferior.
rows.anchor: وقوله أدنى أي أقرب وأدون كما تقول هذا شيء مقارب أو دون

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra prefers deriving adnā from baseness, with hamza omitted.
rows.anchor: فتركت همزتها وهو اختيار الفراء وحكى الأزهري

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd distinguishes al-danī without hamza, meaning vile, from al-danīʾ with hamza, meaning lewd.
rows.anchor: عن ابن زيد الدني بلا همز الخسيس والدنيء بالهمزة الماجن

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One etymology derives Miṣr from being cut off from its surroundings by cultivation.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم هو من القطع لانقطاعه بالعمارة عما سواه

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Another etymology derives Miṣr from its separation from other places.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال هو مشتق من الفصل بينه وبين غيره

rows.speaker: عدي بن زيد
rows.claim: Adi ibn Zayd's verse depicts the sun making Egypt a clear division between day and night, supporting the separation etymology.
rows.anchor:
وقال عدي بن زيد:
وجاعل الشمس مصرا لا خفاء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍuribat ʿalayhim al-dhilla means humiliation was imposed on them, by analogy with a ruler imposing a tax.
rows.anchor: وضربت عليهم الذلة أي فرضت ووضعت عليهم الذلة وألزموها

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another explanation says they settled in the abode of humiliation, using the idiom of pitching tents.
rows.anchor: وقيل ضربت عليهم الذلة أي حلوا بمنزل الذل والمسكنة مأخوذ من ضرب القباب

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's image of a spider's web spread over someone illustrates the idiom of something being laid upon them.
rows.anchor:
قال الفرزدق:
ضربت عليك العنكبوت بنسجها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhilla derives from the verb meaning to be humbled or low.
rows.anchor: وأما الذلة فمشتقة من قولهم ذل فلان يذل ذلا وذلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maskana derives from miskīn; here it means the humility and lowliness of poverty and need, with forms tamaskana and taskana also used.
rows.anchor: والمسكنة مصدر المسكين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the root sense of bāʾū is equalization.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج أصل ذلك التسوية

rows.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
rows.claim: Ubada ibn al-Samit reports that the Prophet distributed the spoils equally among the recipients, illustrating bāʾūʾan as equal shares.
rows.anchor: روي عن عبادة بن الصامت قال جعل الله تعالى الأنفال إلى نبيه فقسمها بينهم على بواء أي على سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A line of poetry uses bawāʾ for an equal or balanced exchange, while noting that blood is not measured out like goods.
rows.anchor: فيقتل جبرا بامرىء لم يكن له بواأ ولكن لا تكايل بالدم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say bāʾū means they confessed what incurred God's wrath; an anonymous verse uses the verb for admitting fault and sin.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم هو الاعتراف ومعناه أنهم اعترفوا بما يوجب غضب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anger means the will to inflict harm; when attributed to God it means His will to punish the one under wrath.
rows.anchor: والغضب إرادة إيصال الضرر إلى من غضب عليه فإذا أضيف إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nabi derives from nabaʾ, news, because a prophet reports from God.
rows.anchor: والنبي اشتقاقه من النبأ الذي هو الخبر لأنه المخبر عن الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh's evidence that Arabs say nabīʾat suʾ and tanabbaʾa supports the hamzated root and excludes derivation from nabāwa.
rows.anchor: سيبويه زعم أنهم يقولون في تحقير النبوة كان مسيلمة نبيئة سوء

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali says nabāwa means elevation, which is not necessarily prophethood, whereas a messenger from God is precisely described by nabaʾ, news.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: ومما يقوي أنه من النبأ الذي هو الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿtidāʾ is crossing the limit God set for His servants, or any limit of one thing into another.
rows.anchor: والاعتداء تجاوز الحد الذي حده الله لعباده إلى غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yukh’rij is jussive as the answer to an omitted command, understood as asking God and telling Him to bring forth the requested food; the implied conditional is indicated by context.
rows.anchor: قوله يخرج لنا مجزوم لأنه جواب أمر محذوف لأن تقديره أدع لنا ربك وقل له أخرج لنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parse makes yukh’rij jussive after an implicit command lām, as in the cited verse from Ibrahim 14:31.
rows.anchor: وقيل أن تقديره أن يكون يخرج مجزوما بإضمار اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in mimmā is partitive because they sought some of what the earth produces, not everything; the alternative treats it as redundant, but min is added only in negation.
rows.anchor: وقوله مما تنبت الأرض من هنا للتبعيض لأن المراد يخرج لنا بعض ما تنبته الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All canonical readers give Miṣr tanwīn, taking it as an unspecified city since the Israelites were in the wilderness; it may instead mean Egypt proper, a masculine name.
rows.anchor: ونون جميع القراء مصرا لأنه أراد مصرا من الأمصار بغير تعيين

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud is reported to read Miṣr without the alif; it may mean Egypt proper as in Yusuf 12:99, whose name is masculine despite denoting a city, or reflect the written muṣḥaf.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن مسعود أنه قرأ بغير ألف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains that the wrath came upon them because of their disbelief in God's signs.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج معناه والله أعلم الغضب حل بهم بكفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabrisī says dhālika points back to the wrath in bāʾū bi-ghaḍab; the causal phrase is governed by the predicate, and the deleted clause is understood from what follows.
rows.anchor: ذلك إشارة إلى الغضب في قوله وباؤوا بغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He applies the same parsing to dhālika bimā ʿaṣaw, with mā and its clause interpreted as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله { ذلك بما عصوا } فإن ما مع صلته في تأويل المصدر

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd cites poetry with yaqūm jussive without the command lām as evidence for its omission.
rows.anchor:
وأنشد أبو زيد:
فيضحي صريعا ما يقوم لحاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another poetic example has adʿu coordinated with udʿu after omission of the command lām.
rows.anchor:
وأنشد غيره:
فقلت ادعي وأدع فإن أندى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further poetic example makes tafdi jussive with the implied sense li-tafdi.
rows.anchor:
وقال آخر:
محمد تفد نفسك كل نفس

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra states that deleting the command lām is allowed only in poetry, where meter forces it.
rows.anchor: في حلقة الفراء فسمعته يقول لأصحابه لا يجوز حذف لام الأمر إلا في الشعر

rows.speaker: المازني
rows.claim: Al-Mazini challenges al-Farra's claim that deletion is poetic necessity because the line could instead say fa-lyadun minni.
rows.anchor: المازني قال جلست في حلقة الفراء فسمعته يقول لأصحابه لا يجوز حذف لام الأمر إلا في الشعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After listing God's favors to the Israelites, the passage recounts their ingratitude and disobedient choice.
rows.anchor: لما عدد سبحانه فيما قبل ما أسداه إليهم من النعم والإحسان ذكر ما قابلوا به تلك النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The addressees of the recollection are the Israelites' forebears.
rows.anchor: أي قال أسلافكم من بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They say they cannot endure one food: manna and quails are called one because the same daily food repeated from day to day, even if it offered varieties.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال على طعام واحد وإن كان طعامهم المن والسلوى وهما شيئان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative account says only manna first descended; they tired of it and then quails were sent.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه كان ينزل عليهم المن وحده فملوه فقالوا ذلك فأنزل عليهم السلوى من بعد ذلك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the people were shaded by clouds and given manna and quails in the wilderness, tired of them, recalled life in Egypt, and asked Moses for its produce.
rows.anchor: ما رواه قتادة قال كان القوم في البرية قد ظلل عليهم الغمام وأنزل عليهم المن والسلوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says they sought produce so the poor could assist the rich, rather than having everyone equally rich and independent.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنهم قالوا لا نصبر على الغنى بأن يكون جميعنا أغنياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes Moses ask whether they exchange the better food God chose for what is lower and worse; another makes God say it.
rows.anchor: معناه قال لهم موسى وقيل بل قال الله لهم أتتركون ما اختار الله لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation contrasts farmed and crafted food with manna and quails given freely.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه أراد أتستبدلون ما تتبذلون في زراعته وصناعته بما أعطاه الله إياكم عفوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading of adnā is the lower-priced choice in place of the more valuable, tasty one.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد تختارون الذي هو أقرب أي أقل قيمة على الذي هو أكثر قيمته وألذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says their request was no sin because they asked for another permissible food; Ṭabrisī prefers the view that it was sinful because they rejected God's choice and were reproached.
rows.anchor: واختلف في سؤالهم هذا هل كان معصية فقيل لم يكن معصية لأن الأول كان مباحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The more apt view is that the request was sinful because they were reproached for refusing what God chose.
rows.anchor: وهو أوجه

rows.speaker: الحسن والربيع
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Rabiʿ say the requested Egypt is Pharaoh's Egypt from which the Israelites departed.
rows.anchor: فقال الحسن والربيع أراد مصر فرعون الذين خرجوا منه

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم وابن زيد
rows.claim: Abu Muslim, with a report also attributed to Ibn Zayd, identifies Egypt as Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم أراد بيت المقدس وروي ذلك عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: قتادة والسدي ومجاهد
rows.claim: Qatada, al-Suddi, and Mujahid take miṣr as any city: the requested crops are found in towns, not in the wilderness.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة والسدي ومجاهد أراد مصرا من الأمصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, the speech ends with the promise that the produce they requested would be available in a settled city; the verse then begins a new account of Sabbath violators and prophet-killers.
rows.anchor: وقد تم الكلام ها هنا ثم استأنف حكم الذين اعتدوا في السبت ومن قتل الأنبياء

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada interpret the humiliation as the subjection expressed in paying jizya under Quran 9:29.
rows.anchor: [التوبة: 29] عن الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata says the humiliation refers to the Jewish kistīj, a distinctive belt and dress.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو الكستيج وزي اليهود عن عطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maskana means the appearance of poverty; even their wealthy people feign destitution lest the tax be doubled.
rows.anchor: يعني زي الفقر فترى المثري منهم يتباءس مخافة أن يضاعف عليه الجزية

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some argue this verse shows wealth's merit because it condemns poverty.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم هذه الآية تدل على فضل الغنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabrisī says that is not the right interpretation: the blame is for poverty of heart, since Jews can be materially wealthy yet spiritually needy; the Prophet says true wealth is of the soul.
rows.anchor: لأن المراد به فقر القلب

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that true wealth is wealth of the soul.
rows.anchor: الغنى غنى النفس

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God exchanged the Jews' honor for humiliation, prosperity for misery, and approval for anger, as requital for disbelief and unjust killing of prophets.
rows.anchor: أبدل الله اليهود بالعز ذلا وبالنعمة بؤسا وبالرضا عنهم غضبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They returned bearing God's anger, which was due upon them and had overtaken them.
rows.anchor: أي رجعوا منصرفين متحملين غضب الله قد وجب عليهم من الله الغضب

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some explain the wrath as worldly affliction and retribution replacing ease and blessing.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: الغضب هو ما حل بهم في الدنيا من البلاء والنقمة

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others take the wrath as punishment for their sins in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون هو ما ينالهم في الآخرة من العقاب على معاصيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhālika points back to the wrath, humiliation, and poverty already mentioned as caused by their disbelief in God's signs.
rows.anchor: فقال { ذلك } أي ذلك الغضب وضرب الذلة والمسكنة حل بهم لأجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation takes God's signs to mean the Gospel and Quran, making the first wrath for rejecting Jesus and the Gospel and a second for rejecting Muhammad and the Quran; another takes them as Muhammad's attributes.
rows.anchor: وقيل أراد بآيات الله الإنجيل والقرآن ولذلك قال فباءوا بغضب على غضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Killing the prophets without right means without any offense, as in the killings of Zechariah and John.
rows.anchor: أي بغير جرم كزكريا ويحيى وغيرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qualifier 'without right' does not imply that prophets could ever be killed justly; it emphasizes that their killing was sheer injustice, like the cited Quranic and poetic examples.
rows.anchor: لا يدل على أنه قد يصح أن يقتل النبيون بحق لأن هذا خرج مخرج الصفة لقتلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhālika bimā ʿaṣaw refers to their Sabbath violation and killing prophets, or to breaking the covenant and assaulting prophets; God acted against them for disobedience and transgression.
rows.anchor: ذلك إشارة إلى ما تقدم أيضا بعصيانهم في قتل الأنبياء وعدوهم السبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God allowed prophets to be killed so they could attain ranks unavailable otherwise; allowing murder of believers and righteous people likewise does not mean God has abandoned them.
rows.anchor: إنما جاز ذلك لتنال أنبياء الله سبحانه من رفع المنازل والدرجات ما لا ينالونه بغير القتل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says God never ordered a prophet to fight and then be killed in battle; those killed were killed outside combat.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى لم يأمر نبيا بالقتال فقتل فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭabrisī's preferred view is that God may not allow a prophet's death before he completes his assigned revelation, since that would undermine the obligations and their benefits; once he has delivered it, God may allow his killers and need not prevent it.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن النبي إن كان لم يؤد الشرع الذي أمر بتأديته لم يجز أن يمكن الله سبحانه من قتله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that Israelites divided 500 years after Moses, when captive-born offspring had become numerous, and divided again 200 years after Jesus.
rows.anchor: اختلفت بنو إسرائيل بعد موسى بخمسمائة سنة حتى كثر فيهم أولاد السبايا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Safīh, jāhil, and ghabī are near-synonyms: foolish, ignorant, and dull.
rows.anchor: السفيه والجاهل والغبي نظائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wallāhu ʿan means he turned someone away; the root walī is closeness and succession without a gap, and the directional forms indicate turning toward versus away.
rows.anchor: واشتقاقه من الولي وهو القرب وهو حصول الثاني بعد الأول من غير فصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qibla first meant the posture or direction in which one thing faces another, then became the name for the direction faced in prayer.
rows.anchor: ثم صار علما على الجهة التي تستقبل في الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the syntax, min al-nās is a circumstantial phrase modifying al-sufahāʾ; mā is an interrogative subject, wallāhum its predicate, and ʿan qiblatihim the complement of wallā.
rows.anchor: من الناس في محل النصب حال من السفهاء وما استفهام وهو مبتدأ وولاهم خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage turns to those who criticized Muslims for shifting from Jerusalem to the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر سبحانه الذين عابوا المسلمين بالانصراف عن قبلة بيت المقدس إلى الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fools are ignorant people among humanity, namely unbelievers.
rows.anchor: أي سوف يقول الجهال وهم الكفار الذين هم بعض الناس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others identify the critics as Jews.
rows.anchor: اختلف في الذين قالوا ذلك فقال ابن عباس وغيره هم اليهود

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the critics were Arab polytheists, who accused Muhammad of leaving his fathers' qibla and then returning to it, and taunted him to return to their religion.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن هم مشركو العرب

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says hypocrites said it to mock Islam.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي هم المنافقون قالوا ذلك استهزاء بالإسلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One motive was to object to abrogation of the former qibla.
rows.anchor: فقيل إنهم قالوا على وجه الإنكار للنسخ عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report says critics promised to follow and believe Muhammad if he returned to their qibla, intending to tempt him away.
rows.anchor: يا محمد ما ولاك عن قبلتك التي كنت عليها ارجع إلى قبلتنا نتبعك ونؤمن بك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view says Arab polytheists made the taunt to suggest that truth lay with their own practice.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنما قاله مشركو العرب ليوهموا أن الحق ما هم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for the qibla change is that God knew it would alter what served people's interests.
rows.anchor: أنه لما علم الله تعالى في ذلك من تغير المصلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is the verse's test: in Mecca facing Jerusalem distinguished Muslims from Kaaba-facing polytheists; in Medina facing the Kaaba distinguished them from Jews facing Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: لأنهم كانوا بمكة أمروا أن يتوجهوا إلى بيت المقدس ليتميزوا من المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God owns both east and west and directs them as wisdom requires, answering those who objected to leaving Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: المشرق والمغرب ملك الله سبحانه يتصرف فيهما كيف شاء على ما تقتضيه حكمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This refutes the claim that the Holy Land is more deserving as the prayer direction because prophets lived there: all places belong to God, who sanctifies whichever He wills at each time for people's interests.
rows.anchor: فرد الله سبحانه عليهم بأن المواطن كلها لله يشرف منها ما يشاء في كل زمان

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وحفص عن عاصم
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Ibn Amir, and Hafs from Asim read raʾūf on the faʿūl pattern; Abu Jaʿfar reads a doubled form without hamza, and the rest use another pattern.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وحفص عن عاصم لرؤوف على وزن رعوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faʿūl reading is supported by that pattern's greater frequency than faʿil and by divine attributes such as ghafūr, shakūr, and wadūd.
rows.anchor: وجه من قرأ رؤوف أن بناء فعول أكثر في كلامهم من فعل

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك الأنصاري
rows.claim: Kaʿb ibn Malik's line uses raʾūfan as evidence for the reading.
rows.anchor:
وقال كعب بن مالك الأنصاري:
نطيع نبينا ونطيع ربا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading of raʾūf is described as prevalent among the people of the Hijaz.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ رؤوفا قال إن ذلك الغالب على أهل الحجاز

rows.speaker: الوليد بن عقبة
rows.claim: Al-Walid ibn Uqba's line to Muawiya uses al-raʾūf al-raḥīm as poetic evidence for the form.
rows.anchor:
قال الوليد بن عقبة لمعاوية:
وشر الطالبين فلا تكنه

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarir's line compares the addressee to a compassionate parent, using al-raʾūf al-raḥīm.
rows.anchor:
وقال جرير:
يرى للمسلمين عليك حقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wasaṭ means just or the best; both meanings converge because the just person is the best, and other explanations derive it from the middle between extremes or from being equidistant from the edges.
rows.anchor: الوسط العدل وقيل الخيار ومعناهما واحد لأن العدل خير عدل

rows.speaker: مؤرج
rows.claim: Muʾarrij glosses ummatan wasaṭan as a community between people and their prophets.
rows.anchor: قال مؤرج: أي وسطا بين الناس وبين أنبيائهم

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr's verse calls a people wasat because others accept their judgment, illustrating their excellence.
rows.anchor:
قال زهير:
هم وسط يرضى الأنام بحكمهم

rows.speaker: صاحب العين
rows.claim: The author of al-ʿAyn defines the middle of anything as its most balanced and best part.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب العين الوسط من كل شيء أعدله وأفضله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wāsiṭ and wasaṭ are alternative forms, like yābis and yabs; calling the Prophet the wasaṭ of his people means he was among their best.
rows.anchor: وقيل الواسط والوسط كما قيل اليابس واليبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAqib means the back of the foot and also a person's descendants; returning on one's heels is also used for turning back.
rows.anchor: والعقب مؤخر القدم وعقب الإنسان نسله

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab explains returning on one's heels as doing evil after good.
rows.anchor:
قال ثعلب:
نرد على أعقابنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAqaba can mean another round in riding or walking; taʿqīb is returning to a desired matter, and the night succeeds the day.
rows.anchor: والعقبة الكرة بعد الكرة في الركوب والمشي والتعقيب الرجوع إلى أمر تريده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḍāʿa means loss or waste; ḍayʿa can mean a person's occupation or dependents, and its root sense is destruction.
rows.anchor: وأصل الضياع الهلاك

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd says raʾaftu and raʾuftu both mean that one showed compassion.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد رأفت بالرجل أرأف به رأفة ورؤفت به أرؤف به بمعنى

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufans parse in this position as mā and the lām as illā, yielding 'it was only great'; the Basrans reject this because the same lām cannot make a nominative Zayd an exception.
rows.anchor: وقال الكوفيون أن في مثل هذا الموضع بمعنى ما واللام بمعنى الا

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: The Basrans reject the Kufan parsing because it would wrongly license a construction such as jāʾa al-qawmu li-Zaydan to mean all came except Zayd.
rows.anchor: وأنكر البصريون ذلك لأنه لو كان كذلك لجاز أن يقال جاء القوم لزيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In mā kāna Allāhu liyuḍīʿa īmānakum, lām reinforces the negation; the verb has an implicit an, which cannot be stated because the phrase is construed as 'God was not one who wasted your faith.'
rows.anchor: فلام تأكيد نفي وأصلها لام الاضافة أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The k of kadhālika is a simile in the accusative as a verbal noun and points back to God's guidance; making the community just is a favor like that guidance.
rows.anchor: والكاف في قوله وكذلك كاف التشبيه وهو في موضع النصب بالمصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative phrase means those whom God guided, with its pronoun omitted; 'except those guided by God' is an exception to the statement that the change was difficult.
rows.anchor: والضمير العائد إلى الموصول محذوف فتقديره على الذين هداهم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage explains the excellence of Muhammad's community over other communities: God made his community just and an intermediary between the Messenger and the people.
rows.anchor: ثم بين سبحانه فضل هذه الأمة على سائر الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though not every member fits the description, it applies to those who do; each age contains a group with this quality.
rows.anchor: أن المراد به من كان بتلك الصفة ولأن كل عصر يخلو من جماعة هذه صفتهم

rows.speaker: بريد بن معاوية العجلي
rows.claim: Al-Baqir says, in a report from Burayd ibn Muawiya al-Ijli, that the Imams are the middle community, God's witnesses over creation and His proof on earth.
rows.anchor: وروى بريد ابن معاوية العجلي عن الباقر ع نحن الأمة الوسط

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: A second report from al-Baqir says the extremists return to the Imams and the deficient catch up through them.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أخرى قال إلينا يرجع الغالي وبنا يلحق المقصر

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali, in a report transmitted through Sulaym ibn Qays, says God meant the Prophet's household: the Prophet witnesses over them, they witness over creation, and they are God's proof on earth.
rows.anchor: عن سليم بن قيس الهلالي عن علي ع: أن الله تعالى إيانا عنى بقوله لتكونوا شهداء على الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the community witnesses to people's deeds that opposed truth in this world and the next, with Quranic parallels in al-Zumar and Ghafir.
rows.anchor: أن المعنى لتشهدوا على الناس بأعمالهم التي خالفوا فيها الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited passages about witnesses at judgment support the community's testimony concerning people's deeds.
rows.anchor:
وجيء بالنبيين والشهداء
[الزمر: 69] وقال:
يوم يقوم الأشهاد
[غافر: 51]

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd counts four sets of witnesses: angels, prophets, Muhammad's community, and bodily limbs, citing the verse about tongues, hands, and feet testifying.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد الأشهاد أربعة الملائكة والأنبياء وأمة محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes the community proof against people by explaining the truth and religion, while the Messenger witnesses by conveying the religion; witness is named for clarifying evidence.
rows.anchor: أن المعنى لتكونوا حجة على الناس فتبينوا لهم الحق والدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view says the community testifies for the prophets against nations that denied them, having learned from the Prophet that those prophets delivered their message.
rows.anchor: أنهم يشهدون للأنبياء على أممهم المكذبين لهم بأنهم قد بلغوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger is said to witness your deeds, or to be a proof against you, or to testify for you at Judgment that your testimony was true; ʿalā can mean li, as in slaughter for idols.
rows.anchor: وقيل حجة عليكم وقيل شهيدا لكم بأنكم قد صدقتم يوم القيامة
